title: Miscarriage: Diagnosis, Causes, Management
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Miscarriage is the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation. It is a common complication, often due to chromosomal abnormalities. Clinical presentation varies from threatened to complete miscarriage, requiring careful diagnosis and management.

sections.p: Miscarriage is defined as the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation or with a fetal weight less than 500 grams. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical signs, physical examination, and imaging. It is crucial to differentiate between types of miscarriage to guide appropriate management.
b: Threatened miscarriage: Vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix and viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Inevitable miscarriage: Vaginal bleeding with an open cervix, but no tissue passed yet. This miscarriage cannot be stopped.
Incomplete miscarriage: Vaginal bleeding with an open cervix and some, but not all, products of conception passed.
Complete miscarriage: All products of conception have been expelled, cervix is closed, and bleeding has subsided.
Missed miscarriage: Fetal death has occurred, but no symptoms of expulsion (bleeding, pain) are present; cervix is closed.
Recurrent miscarriage: Three or more consecutive spontaneous pregnancy losses before 20 weeks.

sections.p: Miscarriage is not typically staged in numerical 'stages' like cancer. Instead, its severity is classified by the clinical presentation and whether the process is ongoing, complete, or complicated. The key determinants are the viability of the pregnancy, cervical status, and the presence of retained products of conception.
b: Threatened: Least severe, potential for continuation.
Inevitable/Incomplete: Active process, requires intervention.
Complete: Process resolved, usually no further intervention needed.
Missed: Requires intervention to remove non-viable pregnancy.
Septic miscarriage: Most severe, involves infection, can be life-threatening.

sections.p: The majority of early miscarriages are due to factors intrinsic to the embryo, while later miscarriages often have maternal or environmental causes. In low-resource settings, infections and nutritional deficiencies can play a more significant role.
b: Chromosomal abnormalities (most common, especially in early miscarriage): Errors at fertilisation lead to non-viable embryos.
Uterine abnormalities: Bicornuate uterus, uterine fibroids, Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions).
Cervical incompetence: Weak cervix dilates prematurely in the second trimester.
Endocrine disorders: Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunction, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
Infections: Malaria, HIV, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, bacterial vaginosis. These are particularly relevant in East African settings.
Immunological factors: Antiphospholipid syndrome.
Thrombophilias: Inherited or acquired clotting disorders.
Environmental factors: Smoking, alcohol, certain drugs, exposure to toxins.
Trauma: Severe physical injury.

sections.p: The presentation of miscarriage varies depending on the type and gestational age. Common symptoms include vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain, but their character helps differentiate the diagnosis.
b: Vaginal bleeding: Can range from spotting to heavy bleeding with clots and tissue. Heavy bleeding is a red flag.
Abdominal pain: Often cramping, suprapubic, or radiating to the back. Can be mild to severe.
Passage of tissue: May describe clots or fleshy material.
Absence of fetal heart tones: On ultrasound, in cases of missed or complete miscarriage.
Symptoms of pregnancy subsiding: Nausea, breast tenderness may decrease.
Fever and foul-smelling discharge: Suggestive of septic miscarriage, a medical emergency.

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm pregnancy, assess viability, determine the type of miscarriage, and rule out complications or alternative diagnoses like ectopic pregnancy. Availability of tests may vary in low-resource settings.

t.b: Confirms pregnancy. A positive result indicates pregnancy, but not viability or location. If unavailable, clinical suspicion and history are key.

Measures pregnancy hormone levels and their trend. A rising level suggests a viable pregnancy, while falling or plateauing levels suggest miscarriage or ectopic. Serial measurements are more informative than a single value. Often unavailable in low-resource settings.

Visualises the uterus and adnexa to confirm intrauterine pregnancy, fetal viability (fetal heart activity), gestational age, and presence of retained products of conception. Also rules out ectopic pregnancy. If TVUS is unavailable, transabdominal ultrasound may be used, though less sensitive in early pregnancy.
Assesses for anaemia due to blood loss and signs of infection (leukocytosis). Essential for assessing patient stability.
Determines need for anti-D immunoglobulin in Rh-negative women to prevent sensitisation.
If infection is suspected (e.g., septic miscarriage), to identify causative organisms and guide antibiotic choice. Often unavailable; empirical antibiotics may be started.
If heavy bleeding or suspected coagulopathy, to assess clotting function. Often unavailable; clinical assessment of bleeding is crucial.

sections.p: Certain signs indicate severe complications requiring immediate attention. Failure to recognise these can lead to significant morbidity and mortality, especially in settings with limited resources.
b: Heavy vaginal bleeding: Soaking more than one pad per hour, signs of hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension).
Severe abdominal pain: Unrelieved by analgesia, signs of peritonitis.
Fever and chills: Suggestive of septic miscarriage, especially with foul-smelling discharge.
Syncope or dizziness: Indicative of significant blood loss.
Retained products of conception: Can lead to ongoing bleeding, infection, or Asherman's syndrome.
Septic miscarriage: Life-threatening infection of the uterus and surrounding tissues.
Haemorrhage: Excessive blood loss leading to anaemia or hypovolaemic shock.
Psychological impact: Grief, anxiety, depression; often overlooked.

sections.p: Management depends on the type of miscarriage, gestational age, patient preference, and available resources. The goals are to ensure complete expulsion of products of conception, control bleeding, prevent infection, and provide emotional support.
b: Expectant management: For threatened or complete miscarriage, or stable incomplete/missed miscarriage. Monitor for spontaneous expulsion. Suitable if no signs of infection or heavy bleeding.

Medical management: Misoprostol (prostaglandin E1 analogue) is used to induce uterine contractions and expel products of conception. Effective for incomplete or missed miscarriage. Avoid in cases of suspected ectopic or allergy.

Surgical management: Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) or Dilatation and Curettage (D&C). Indicated for heavy bleeding, signs of infection, haemodynamic instability, or failed medical/expectant management. MVA is preferred in low-resource settings due to its simplicity and lower cost.
Anti-D immunoglobulin: Administer to Rh-negative women after any miscarriage to prevent Rh sensitisation.

Antibiotics: Prophylactic antibiotics may be given before surgical management. Therapeutic antibiotics are crucial for septic miscarriage (e.g., broad-spectrum such as ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole).
Pain management: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) and opioids (e.g., tramadol) as needed.
Emotional support: Counselling and psychological support are vital for women experiencing miscarriage.

sections.p: Follow-up is essential to ensure complete resolution, address complications, and provide guidance for future pregnancies. Prevention strategies focus on identifying and managing underlying risk factors.
b: Follow-up visit: To confirm complete expulsion (e.g., with ultrasound or declining hCG), assess for complications, and provide contraception advice.
Counselling for recurrent miscarriage: Investigate underlying causes (e.g., chromosomal analysis, antiphospholipid syndrome screening, uterine anomaly assessment).
Lifestyle modifications: Avoid smoking, alcohol, and illicit drugs. Maintain a healthy weight.
Management of chronic conditions: Optimize control of diabetes, thyroid disorders, and hypertension.
Infection screening and treatment: Especially for STIs and malaria in endemic areas.
Folic acid supplementation: Before conception and in early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects, though not directly preventing miscarriage.

sections.p: Distinguishing miscarriage from other conditions presenting with similar symptoms is critical for correct diagnosis and management, especially in early pregnancy.
b: Ectopic pregnancy: Presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain, but the pregnancy is outside the uterus. Can be life-threatening. Ultrasound and serial hCG are key differentiators.

Molar pregnancy (Hydatidiform mole): Abnormal placental growth, can present with bleeding and uterine enlargement greater than dates. Ultrasound shows characteristic 'snowstorm' appearance. Can lead to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
Normal early pregnancy bleeding: Some women experience light spotting in early pregnancy without miscarriage. Diagnosis relies on ultrasound confirming a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Cervical or vaginal lesions: Bleeding from polyps, cervicitis, or trauma can mimic miscarriage symptoms.
Urinary tract infection (UTI): Can cause abdominal discomfort, but typically without significant bleeding or passage of tissue.

sections.p: Interpreting clinical and investigative findings requires careful consideration, as some results can be ambiguous or falsely reassuring, leading to misdiagnosis or delayed intervention.
b: Negative urine pregnancy test: Can be falsely negative in very early pregnancy or with dilute urine. Always repeat if clinical suspicion is high.
Low or plateauing beta-hCG: Can indicate miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy. Requires correlation with ultrasound findings and clinical picture.

Empty uterus on ultrasound: In very early pregnancy, an intrauterine gestational sac may not yet be visible, leading to a false suspicion of ectopic or complete miscarriage. Repeat ultrasound is often needed.
Retained products of conception: Ultrasound may not always clearly show small amounts of retained tissue, leading to a false diagnosis of complete miscarriage.
Clinical assessment of blood loss: Can be underestimated by patients or clinicians, leading to delayed intervention for haemorrhage.
Symptoms of pregnancy subsiding: Can be a normal variation, not always indicative of missed miscarriage.

whenToSeekHelp: Heavy vaginal bleeding (soaking more than one pad per hour)

faq.a: Most early miscarriages due to chromosomal abnormalities are not preventable. However, managing underlying maternal conditions like diabetes or thyroid disease, and avoiding harmful substances, can reduce risks for some types of miscarriage.

faq.q: How soon can I try to conceive after a miscarriage?
faq.a: Physically, most women can try to conceive after their first normal menstrual period. Emotionally, it's important to allow time for grief and healing. Discuss with your doctor for personalised advice.

faq.q: What is the difference between threatened and inevitable miscarriage?
faq.a: Threatened miscarriage involves vaginal bleeding with a closed cervix and a viable pregnancy, meaning it might continue. Inevitable miscarriage also has bleeding, but the cervix is open, indicating the miscarriage cannot be stopped.

exam: A 28-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain at 10 weeks gestation. On examination, her cervix is open, but no tissue has been passed. What is your diagnosis and immediate management plan? — Diagnosis: Inevitable miscarriage. Immediate management: Assess haemodynamic stability, pain relief, blood group and Rh status, offer medical (misoprostol) or surgical (MVA) management, and provide emotional support.

You are in a rural clinic with no ultrasound. A 20-year-old presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and passage of tissue after 12 weeks of amenorrhoea. What clinical signs would lead you to suspect an incomplete miscarriage, and what is your immediate action? — Clinical signs: Heavy bleeding, open cervix, palpable retained products of conception, uterine size smaller than expected for gestational age but larger than a complete miscarriage. A patient treated for an incomplete miscarriage two weeks ago now presents with fever, foul-smelling discharge, and abdominal pain. What is your most likely diagnosis and how would you manage this in a low-resource setting? — Diagnosis: Septic miscarriage. Management: ABCs, IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole), prompt evacuation of retained products of conception (MVA/D&C) once stabilised, monitor for signs of sepsis/shock.

A 35-year-old woman has experienced three consecutive miscarriages. What investigations would you consider to determine the cause of her recurrent pregnancy loss? — Investigations: Parental karyotyping, antiphospholipid antibody testing, thyroid function tests, screening for diabetes, hysteroscopy or hysterosalpingography to assess for uterine anomalies (e.g., bicornuate uterus, Asherman's syndrome), and cervical length assessment in subsequent pregnancies.

Why is it crucial to administer anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative women after a miscarriage, and when should it be given? — It prevents Rh sensitisation, where the mother's immune system produces antibodies against fetal Rh-positive blood cells, which can cause haemolytic disease in future Rh-positive pregnancies. It should be given within 72 hours of the miscarriage or any potentially sensitising event.

A patient presents with amenorrhoea after treatment for an incomplete miscarriage. What is a potential long-term complication related to the uterine cavity, and how would you investigate it? — Potential complication: Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions). Investigation: Hysteroscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis, or hysterosalpingography if hysteroscopy is unavailable.
